headline: As the author of the “Iskander-1000” designation, the MilitaryRussia project felt the need to comment on the information released by Ukraine’s Main Directorate of Intelligence (GUR/HUR) about its alleged first use against targets in Ukraine. The claim is based on the discovery of missile remnants bearing the 9M723-2 designation. Here’s the important part: 1. 9M723-2 and 9M723-2F3 are NOT the “Iskander-1000” with an extended range. This comes down to how Soviet/Russian missile designations work. The 9M723 designation refers to the missile/rocket section, while the warhead has its own designation. Different warheads can be fitted to the same missile section. For example, the 9M723K5 consists of the 9M723 missile section fitted with the 9N722K5 warhead. Information available from 2011 mentioned two missile-section variants: 9M723 and 9M723-1. A new version, provisionally designated 9M723-2, appeared in 2024. MilitaryRussia initially used the 9M723-2 designation in 2024 to identify what it called the “Iskander-1000”, a proposed extended-range version of the Iskander. They now consider that identification to have been incorrect. Based on the available information, the more likely breakdown is: • 9M723 — an earlier missile section with a clearly visible cable channel along the body. • 9M723-1 — a more conventional design, with six decoys located in the rear section. • 9M723-2 — a newer design without the six decoys, but with additional antenna modules associated with the satellite-navigation system. 2. What about the reported 800 km launch? On December 18, 2025, Ukrainian media reported a missile launch to a range of around 800 km. MilitaryRussia believes this may have been a test launch of the actual “Iskander-1000” using the standard Iskander launcher. 3. So what exactly is the 9M723-2? At this point, there are two main possibilities. It could be a simplified and lighter version of the 9M723-1 of the 9K720 “Iskander-M” system. Also, it could be a newer version designed to provide better accuracy and greater resistance to electronic warfare. For now, this is still speculation. The secrecy surrounding new Russian missile developments, combined with the lack of clear photographic evidence from the crash sites, means there is not enough information to draw firm conclusions.

headline: CIA Director Visit to Russia, Reasons, and Forecast (General Access) ICOD-1110, 08/28/2026 BLUF: On Tuesday, August 25, 2026, CIA Director John Ratcliffe made a surprise visit to Russia to meet with his Russian counterpart, Russian Foreign Intelligence Service Director Sergei Naryshkin. While Russian news and official outlets characterized the meeting as 'contacts' with their U.S. intelligence counterparts, declining to elaborate on what was said, amidst increased Russian hybrid and direct actions against European nations, U.S. news outlets were told by U.S. and European officials that the meeting was set to warn Russia against attacking a NATO partner, urge them to reenter Russo-Ukrainian peace talks, and distance themselves from Iran. This has prompted many to double down on reports that Russia may have been planning a direct military action against a NATO member state in the near term. Key Points: - U.S. President Donald J. Trump personally dispatched Director Ratcliffe to Russia, keeping both his counterparts in Europe and some top U.S. officials and administration aides in the dark on the matter. This caused a general scramble of diplomatic communications and wider speculation when Ratcliffe's C-17 was seen flying into Russia. - Intelligence suggested that Russia may have been preparing a direct, albeit limited, action against ba NATO member state. - Two primary rundowns of what was communicated to Russia have come out: • That NATO Article 5 commitments remain robust (in effect warning Russia against attacking a NATO member state), that Russo-Ukrainian peace/ceasefire processes should be restarted, and that Russia must distance itself from Iran. • That the primary purpose of the meeting was to communicate Russia's inability to decisively win a largely stalemated war with Ukraine. (various casualty, industry, and other metrics were reportedly cited.) - Hybrid actions indirectly attributed to the Russians and/or directly traced to them have increased notably in the past months with a number of notable incidents, including a potential clandestine sabotage mission against a German military facility, stopped by Serbian authorities; cyberwarfare activities against France; and numerous drones shot down and drone impacts in both Romania and the Baltics. - ISR was increasingly active around the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad in the days/week leading up to the visit. Analyst Comment Additional reports that Russian President Vladimir Putin may be pushed to execute a limited tactical nuclear strike have been factored into this assessment but do not weigh heavily on our I&W tree. Assessment: The aforementioned dynamic, coupled with the largely stalemated battlefield dynamic of the ongoing Russo-Ukrainian War, has led some to believe that, seeking to implement an 'escalate to deescalate' strategy, Russian President Vladimir Putin may be looking to escalate against NATO as a means to cause a fracture within NATO and possibly expose NATO's Article 5 defense clause as largely a bluff, which would in turn aid in his primary venture of the war in Ukraine. As mentioned in the "Key Points" portion of this assessment, there are two prevailing characterizations of the intelligence meeting on the 25th, but that does not mean both cannot be true at the same time, as the Trump administration has been keen to publicly isolate Iran economically and diplomatically and realize a U.S.-brokered settlement of the Russo-Ukrainian War, while simultaneously, Russian actions against NATO member states have been increasing. Additionally, the meeting this past week with the policy heads of NATO member states, including U.S. Under Secretary of War for Policy Elbridge Colby, where key new and to-be-renewed NATO force model and policy frameworks were set to be discussed, also likely plays some part in the timing of the meeting. Key Judgement: - It's currently highly unlikely that Russia is seeking to use tactical nuclear weapons on the battlefield in Ukraine in the near-term, as Russian tactical nuclear use, from a doctrinal perspective, is meant to forestall a significant collapse of Russian forces on the battlefield, something that is not currently happening. - A Russian attack on a NATO member state is currently unlikely in the near-term, as Russian readiness is not currently at a level to withstand the potential NATO response should Article 5 be implemented. Additionally, per Western news outlets, Baltic intelligence agencies currently assess the likelihood of such a move by Russia against them in the near-term as low. - As assessed in previous assessments, barring significant concessions, it's still unlikely that Russian president Vladimir Putin will seriously reenter talks to end the ongoing Russo-Ukrainian war. - Barring a more robust European response to Russian hybrid actions, it's unlikely that a warning alone, even that from the CIA director, will avert Russia from its current course of action as it relates to grey-zone operations against nations that support Ukraine. END

headline: China is rapidly expanding the Lop Nur flight test complex in Xinjiang, a highly restricted facility used for testing advanced and experimental military aircraft. Lop Nur has previously been associated with testing China's J-36 and J-XDS sixth generation fighter designs. The latest construction is particularly notable because the new southern hangars are substantially wider than typical tactical-aircraft shelters. The War Zone assesses that the facilities could eventually support larger aircraft, including China's H-20 stealth bomber, which has yet to publicly appear. However, the article emphasizes that there is currently no evidence the H-20 is headed to Lop Nur, making that an assessment rather than a confirmed development. The broader takeaway is that Lop Nur is evolving from a relatively austere test airfield into a major, high capacity test center for China's next generation aerospace programs, with the pace of construction accelerating significantly in 2025–26. Source: https://www.twz.com/news-features/chinas-area-51-is-undergoing-a-massive-expansion

headline: Ukraine has received intelligence that Russia is planning a new ground offensive from Belarus against the capital of Kyiv and Chernihiv, while Moscow ramps up drone and missile strikes on cities throughout Ukraine, according to a report by POLITICO. Speaking Saturday to reporters, Pavlo Palisa, the Deputy Head of Ukraine’s Presidential Office, said that Russian military leadership had been tasked by the Kremlin with planning and preparing for attacks on the two cities, via intelligence received and verified by Ukraine’s Main Directorate of Intelligence. So far, Palisa states, evidence does not suggest that Russian ground forces are massing in Belarus and Western Russia for such an operation, but that Ukraine’s priority is to “prevent the creation of conditions for the Russians to be able to launch any offensive actions at all.” At the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, Russian ground forces attempted an offensive on Kyiv, launched in part from nearby Belarus, but ultimately became bogged down due to strikes on logistics lines before being crushed and repelled by the Armed Forces of Ukraine. Since then, the Russian Army has been significantly weakened while the Ukrainian Army has only grown stronger, even making small gains against Russia in Eastern Ukraine.

headline: The Iran war is creating growing concerns about U.S. munitions inventories and the ability to respond to a major contingency involving China or Russia. According to U.S. officials cited by the Wall Street Journal, PAC-3 Patriot interceptors and ATACMS missiles in Europe have fallen to “beyond critical” levels. Other precision weapons and guided rockets have also been drawn down, while THAAD interceptors and counter-drone systems have been moved from Europe to the Middle East. By mid-July, U.S. forces had reportedly expended approximately 1,700 Patriot interceptors, 200 THAAD interceptors and 150 Navy Standard Missiles during the Iran conflict. Iran has launched more than 1,500 ballistic missiles and 6,000 large drones during the war. The depletion is affecting U.S. planning. European Command has reportedly adjusted operational plans, while officials have previously acknowledged that current inventories could constrain the ability to execute contingency plans for Taiwan. The problem is compounded by production timelines. Replenishing some advanced interceptors and missiles could take years, even as European allies face delays receiving weapons they have already purchased. The White House and Pentagon dispute the characterization of a broader U.S. munitions shortage, saying current inventories remain sufficient to meet America's strategic objectives. NATO likewise says the alliance retains enough air-defense munitions for its defense. headline: President Trump says the U.S. has secured majority control over a joint venture covering more than 65 billion barrels of proven Venezuelan oil reserves, following the administration’s effort to bring American energy companies back into Venezuela. Under the reported arrangement, Venezuela’s interim government granted the venture a 100-year concession to operate the affected oil fields. The U.S. government would control 55% of the venture, through a combination of equity and the ability to acquire oil at cost. The Trump administration says the arrangement could bring nearly $100 billion in private investment, increase U.S. oil supplies and eventually reduce energy prices. The administration also says the deal comes at no cost to U.S. taxpayers. The agreement covers roughly one-fifth of Venezuela’s more than 300 billion barrels of proven reserves. Venezuela has the world's largest proven oil reserves, but production has been constrained for years by underinvestment, deteriorating infrastructure, sanctions and the nationalization of foreign-owned assets. The identity of the private operator involved in the joint venture has not yet been disclosed. Companies including Chevron, Repsol and Eni still have operations or interests in Venezuela, while other major oil companies remain wary after having assets nationalized under Hugo Chávez. The deal is part of a broader U.S. effort to reopen Venezuela's oil industry to foreign investment following the January U.S. military operation that removed Nicolás Maduro and installed Delcy Rodríguez as interim president. Source: https://www.cbsnews.com/news/trump-venezuela-oil-u-s-majority-control-65-billion-barrels/
